newsitem.title: USA: U.S. takes issue with Germany on Scientology.
newsitem.headline: U.S. takes issue with Germany on Scientology.

text.p: The United States took issue with Germany on Thursday for discriminating against Scientology in business and cultural life, but said there had also been "some positive developments" in Bonn's treatment of the group.

In its annual human rights report for 1996, the State Department said a "sharp debate" surrounded the activities in Germany of the Church of Scientology, which German officials have portrayed as a potential threat to the public.

The report said German members of the Los Angeles-based church "allege both government-condoned and societal harassment, including expulsion from (or denial of permission to join) a political party and loss of employment."
Businesses whose owners or executives are Scientologists may face boycotts and discrimination, sometimes with government approval, it said.
In Los Angeles, the president of the Church of Scientology International hailed the report as "the most decisive condemnation of German human rights terrorism since the end of World War II."

Rev. Heber Jentzsch said in a statement that the State Department report "strips the artificial veneer from German-style democracy. It exposes these people as having zero justification for their unscrupulous and outrageous hate campaign."

At the same time, he charged Bonn with stepping up retaliation against the Church in Germany, by sending police to the Scientology church in Stuttgart with a decree banning it from handing out food, drink and clothing to homeless people.
Jentzsch branded the decree "a mad act by a spiteful government which got exposed violating its own constitution, international law and the principles of decency."
The report noted that major German political parties excluded Scientologists from membership, arguing that the Church was not a religion but a for-profit organisation with anti-democratic goals.
Artists had been prevented from performing or displaying their works because of membership in the church, it added.

But the report said that "the past year has also seen some positive developments," including an interior ministry finding in October that there was insufficient evidence to justify surveillance of the group by security agencies.
Although much of the report was couched in a neutral, factual tone, some of its observations implied U.S. concern over German treatment of the group.
U.S. officials sidestep the issue of whether Scientology is legally a religion but say the United States accords it religious rights.

Officials said the decision to devote much more space to Scientology in Germany in this year's report than in four previous reports which have mentioned the issue reflected the publicity it has received in the past year.

Scientology is a religious philosophy founded in 1954 by American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard. Several prominent U.S. show business figures including filmstars Tom Cruise and John Travolta and jazz pianist Chick Corea belong to the group.

The State Department has strongly criticised U.S. Scientologists and their Hollywood supporters for newspaper advertisements and statements comparing German treatment of the group to the Nazi persecution of the Jews.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns earlier this week branded the comparison "outrageous."
The human rights report made no mention of this aspect of the controversy.
